analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic rivals to keep cheaper generics off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban pay-for-delay deals never got a committee vote in the 115th Congress; it died with 38 cosponsors and no roll call.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drugmaker challenges a brand-name drug's patents, the two companies sometimes settle with the brand company paying the generic maker to stay off the market for years — a practice known as pay-for-delay. This bill would declare those deals an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, impose civil penalties of up to three times the value received, claw back research tax credits from violators, and stop companies from deducting those penalties on their taxes. It also would require the chief executives of settling companies to certify under oath that they filed the complete agreements with the FTC and the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy prescription drugs or pay insurance premiums. Once a generic enters the market, prices typically drop sharply, and the bill targets the main settlement device brand companies use to postpone that day. Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers also stand to pay less per prescription.

how_it_helps.text: Declares agreements in which a generic maker receives anything of value in exchange for delaying or forgoing sales of its product an unfair method of competition, subject to FTC enforcement [S2][S3]
Imposes a civil penalty of up to three times the value a party received from a violating agreement, and lets the FTC force violators to forfeit that value [S3]
Claws back the research and development tax credit from a manufacturer the FTC finds violated the ban, and bars companies from deducting the resulting civil penalties from their taxes [S2][S3]

Requires the CEO or lead negotiator of a settling company to certify to the FTC and the Justice Department that the filings include all side agreements and oral promises, closing the gap through which undisclosed payments could flow [S3]
Bars the fact finder from presuming that a generic would not have launched before patent expiration, the assumption that historically let delayed-entry settlements escape antitrust scrutiny [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers. They would lose the ability to pay a generic rival to stay off the market, face penalties up to three times the value received, and lose R&D tax credits and tax deductions for the penalties if the FTC finds a violation.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves room for procompetitive settlements: it allows generic makers to receive an exclusive early-entry license and litigation-expense payments up to $7.5 million, and it exempts agreements whose procompetitive benefits outweigh the anticompetitive effects — a fact-intensive standard that would take years of FTC cases to settle into predictable rules [S3]

Brand companies and their allies argue that some patent settlements genuinely speed generic entry and that banning compensation will push disputes into full patent litigation, which can itself delay generics for years and raise litigation costs for generic makers [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — faster generic entry and lower drug prices for patients and insurers — is large and direct, since pay-for-delay settlements are the best-documented cause of multi-year delays in generic availability. The main costs fall on brand manufacturers, not patients. The honest objection is enforcement design: the FTC would have to litigate case by case under a procompetitive-exception standard, and outcomes could be slow or inconsistent, and the bill's narrow carve-out for litigation costs and early licenses could be stretched in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on October 25, 2017, with 20 original cosponsors [S1][S3]
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce committees, and to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee two days later [S5]
The bill accumulated 37 cosponsors, all Democrats, but no committee scheduled a hearing or markup and the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S4][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept the ability to settle patent suits by paying generic makers to delay market entry and kept the research tax credits the bill would have clawed back.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 supporters on record — the sponsor and 37 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and every committee chairmanship, the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: These companies have collected years of monopoly-priced sales by paying generic challengers to stay off the market. The bill would ban the practice, impose penalties up to three times the value received, and claw back R&D tax credits, directly cutting into a major profit-protection strategy at the expense of patients' drug bills.

Generic makers lose the option of taking settlement payments for delay, but they gain faster entry to the market and, under the bill's carve-out, can still get exclusive early-launch licenses and litigation-cost payments up to $7.5 million. Earlier entry means they sell more volume sooner.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Faster generic competition lowers the prices insurers and employers pay for prescriptions, though PBM middlemen capture part of the spread between list and net prices.
